title: The Greedy Landlord and the Banyan Shade (HI)
summary: A greedy landlord sells the shade of a banyan tree to a weary traveler, then tries to evict him as the sun moves. Birbal resolves the contract.
full_text:
On a sweltering afternoon in the dusty plains of Malwa, a weary traveling merchant named Govind rested beneath the sprawling, cool shade of an enormous banyan tree on the property of a wealthy landlord named Seth Girdhari.

The greedy landlord approached Govind with a cane: 'This banyan tree is on my private land! If you want to sit in its shade, you must pay me two silver coins!'

Govind, desperate for rest, paid the two silver coins, saying: 'I purchase the right to rest in this tree's shade until sunset.'

Two hours later, as the afternoon sun moved west, the shadow of the giant banyan shifted, stretching across the landlord's garden and touching the veranda of his private mansion. Govind picked up his bundle and moved with the shadow, sitting on the edge of the landlord's veranda.

Girdhari ran out, screaming: 'Get off my veranda! You are trespassing!'

Govind replied calmly: 'I bought the shade of the banyan tree until sunset! The shade has moved onto your veranda, so I have every legal right to sit wherever my shade falls!'

The furious landlord dragged the traveler before Emperor Akbar's imperial court in Agra.

Akbar was amused by the bizarre dispute: 'Can a man buy shade, Birbal?'

Birbal listened to the contract, smiled, and said:

'Seth Girdhari, you sold Govind the complete, unrestricted use of the banyan tree's shade until sunset for two silver coins. A sale is a sale.'

Girdhari protested: 'Yes, but now the shade covers my veranda, my front courtyard, and enters my living room window!'

'Then Govind has the absolute legal right to enter your living room and sit beside your dinner table!' Birbal declared, his eyes twinkling. 'For wherever the shade travels until sunset, the shade belongs to Govind!

'Furthermore, since you are currently occupying a house that is partially covered by Govind's shade, you must either step out of his shade into the blazing sun, or pay Govind a rental fee of twenty gold coins for enjoying his shade!'

The courtiers burst into roaring laughter. Realizing his absurd greed had backfired, Girdhari returned the traveler's silver coins, offered him a feast of sweetmeats, and apologized.

Akbar commended Birbal for using humor to defend the helpless traveler.
